reason: The goal concerns the response to glucose after a meal, and the pancreatic cells sit beside blood vessels, so they seem a likely place to sense it.
expectation: The pancreatic cells will detect the glucose-rich blood and begin a response.

effect: The glucose-rich blood first had to be connected to the body; the pancreatic sensing cells have not been used yet.
reaction: I expected sensing to happen immediately, so the extra connection was a little surprising.
reason: The body now has rising blood glucose, and the pancreatic cells are pictured beside its blood vessels, making them a likely next step for sensing it.
expectation: The pancreatic cells will sense the rise and start a response.

effect: The pancreatic cells responded to rising glucose by releasing insulin into the blood, with routes shown toward muscle and liver.
reaction: It makes more sense now how the pancreas signals other tissues.
reason: The picture shows insulin travelling toward muscle, and skeletal muscle is available to connect to that response.
expectation: The muscle will respond to insulin and take up glucose from the blood.

alternatives.reason: The liver is also shown as a destination for the insulin signal.

effect: Insulin helped muscle take up glucose, and the later picture showed less glucose and insulin in the blood. The next goal is to keep glucose available between meals.
reaction: It was satisfying to see the response reduce the original rise.
reason: Time between meals shows incoming glucose tapering while cells continue using it, matching the new goal.

choice.combine: Body taking up glucose into muscle

expectation: The body will move into a between-meals state with less incoming glucose.

effect: Between meals, blood glucose is falling while the liver still has stored glycogen.
reaction: The clock makes the change in glucose supply clear.
reason: The pancreatic sensing cells responded to rising glucose earlier, so I expect them to respond to the fall too.
expectation: The pancreas will detect the falling glucose and signal a response that helps keep glucose available.

alternatives.reason: The liver's stored glycogen could provide glucose, as shown in the earlier liver chapter.

effect: Falling blood glucose led pancreatic alpha cells to release glucagon, which travels toward the liver.
reaction: The two pancreatic responses now seem connected to different glucose levels.
reason: The glucagon route points toward the liver, and the earlier liver chapter showed glycogen releasing glucose.
expectation: The liver will respond by releasing glucose from its glycogen stores into the blood.

effect: The liver broke down stored glycogen and released glucose into the blood; as glucose rose, glucagon release decreased. Both goals are complete.
reaction: It was satisfying to see how the between-meals response could ease once glucose rose.

mostWorthwhile.text: The liver response was most worthwhile: it connected stored glycogen to keeping glucose available between meals and showed the signal easing afterward.

leastWorthwhile.text: The first attempt was a little confusing: the pancreatic cells seemed ready to sense glucose, but the blood had to be connected to the body first.

surprise.text: I was surprised that the first attempt automatically connected the glucose-rich blood to the body instead of sensing it directly.

arbitrary.text: That initial body connection felt somewhat like a required setup rather than a meaningful biological choice, though the result made the situation clear.

continue.text: I would choose to continue: seeing the meal and between-meal responses side by side made me curious about how the body handles other changes.
